Does neighborhood nature relate to dementia risk?

A 13-year cohort of 426,220 adults links greener surroundings with lower observed risk.

Our everyday environments are designed. What can this published study actually tell us about their relationship with human health and the brain?

The study

Researchers followed 426,220 UK Biobank participants without dementia for a median 13.6 years and studied nearby green and blue space.

The findings

They recorded 3,513 Alzheimer’s cases and 864 cases of mild cognitive impairment. Greener surroundings were associated with lower risks in several models; the observational design cannot prove causation.

What this means for architecture

Green access deserves attention in urban planning, but associations do not show that adding trees prevents dementia.

Conclusion

The evidence points to an important research question, not a universal design rule. Better controlled and longer-term studies are needed.

Liu et al. (2026)

Associations between residential environments and the risk of incident Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive impairment: a 13-year prospective cohort study with 426,220 participants. Aging & Mental Health (2026)
